act-english.title: ACT English — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
act-english.summary: Master grammar, punctuation, and rhetoric to ace 75 questions in 45 minutes across 5 passages.

slides.title: What is ACT English?
points: 75 questions, 45 minutes across 5 passages (~15 min/passage)
Tests grammar, punctuation, sentence structure, and writing strategy
Passages: essays ranging 500–600 words; 15 questions per passage
Score range: 1–36 (converted to composite with other sections)
slides.tip: ACT English is the fastest section — time pressure is real. Build speed through practice.

slides.title: English Section Timing & Pacing
points: ~36 seconds per question average; aim to complete each passage in 10–12 minutes
Read the full sentence/paragraph before answering; context determines correctness
Don't slow down on hard questions — skip and return if time allows
Last 1–2 questions are often the hardest; allocate time accordingly
slides.tip: If you're running behind, guess quickly on rhetorical questions and move on.

slides.title: Grammar & Mechanics Mastery (Part 1)
points: Subject-verb agreement: Verb must match subject in number (singular/plural)
Pronoun agreement: Pronouns must match their antecedent (he/she/it vs. they)
Verb tense consistency: Don't switch tenses mid-narrative without reason
Common trap: Prepositional phrases hide the true subject; ignore them

example.label: Subject-Verb Example
example.text: WRONG: 'The list of mistakes were found.' RIGHT: 'The list of mistakes was found.' (list = singular)

slides.tip: Cross out prepositional phrases (of..., with..., in...) to find subject-verb pairs.

slides.title: Grammar & Mechanics Mastery (Part 2)
points: Comma rules: Use commas for introductory clauses, items in a series, and appositive phrases
Semicolons: Join independent clauses only; NOT before fragments or lists
Colons: Introduce explanations, lists, or independent clauses; use sparingly
Apostrophes: Possessives (john's, cat's) and contractions (it's, they're); NOT 'it' or 'who's'

example.label: Semicolon Trap
example.text: WRONG: 'I love ice cream; especially chocolate.' RIGHT: 'I love ice cream, especially chocolate.' (fragment after colon)

slides.tip: Semicolons and colons are rare in ACT — most ACT punctuation is commas.

slides.title: Sentence Structure & Fragments
points: Fragments: Missing subject, verb, or both — must be joined or completed
Run-ons: Two independent clauses without punctuation/conjunction — fix with comma+and, semicolon, or period
Comma splices: Two independent clauses joined by comma alone — same fixes as run-ons
Parallelism: Series items must match grammatical form (verb parallels verb, noun parallels noun)

example.label: Parallelism Example
example.text: WRONG: 'She likes to run, swim, and playing tennis.' RIGHT: 'She likes to run, swim, and play tennis.' (all gerunds OR all infinitives)

slides.tip: When you see a series, check that all items have the same structure.

slides.title: Modifiers & Misplacement
points: Dangling modifiers: Opening phrase doesn't clearly modify the subject — rewrite or move subject
Misplaced modifiers: Modifier is too far from the word it describes — move it next to the target
Watch for: -ing phrases, 'which' clauses, and introductory prepositional phrases
The subject right after the comma usually gets modified by an introductory phrase

example.label: Dangling Modifier Example
example.text: WRONG: 'Running down the street, the car nearly hit me.' (Who is running? Unclear.) RIGHT: 'As I ran down the street, the car nearly hit me.'

slides.tip: If an introductory phrase doesn't logically modify the subject, it's dangling — fix it.

slides.title: Rhetorical Skills: Strategy & Style (Part 1)
points: ~30% of questions test writing strategy, NOT grammar — no single 'correct' answer, but best fit
Ask: Does the phrase match the tone and purpose of the passage?
Consider: Conciseness, clarity, relevance, and consistency with surrounding sentences
Options often include 'NO CHANGE' — if existing text is clear and appropriate, pick it
slides.tip: Rhetorical questions reward reading the full passage; context is everything.

slides.title: Conciseness & Word Choice
points: Eliminate redundancy: 'very unique' (unique means one-of-a-kind), 'future plans' (plans are future)
Avoid wordiness: 'In the event that' -> 'if'; 'due to the fact that' -> 'because'
Shorter is better: If two choices mean the same thing, pick the shorter one
Watch for: Repetition of ideas, unnecessary adjectives, and awkward phrasing

example.label: Conciseness Example
example.text: WORDY: 'She was afraid and frightened by the dog.' CONCISE: 'She was afraid of the dog.' (afraid = frightened)

slides.tip: On rhetorical questions, eliminate choices that repeat or add nothing new.

slides.title: Tone & Style Consistency
points: Match the passage's register: Formal vs. informal tone must remain consistent
Avoid: Casual slang in academic passages, pretentious language in simple essays
Watch author's voice: Is the passage personal (first person), objective (third person), or mixed?
Check: Verb voice (active vs. passive) — switch only if the passage does

example.label: Tone Mismatch Example
example.text: In a formal essay: WRONG: 'The scientist totally figured out the answer.' RIGHT: 'The scientist determined the answer.'

slides.tip: Read the first 1–2 sentences of each passage to catch its tone — then check new sentences against it.

slides.title: Transitions & Organization
points: Transitions signal relationships: 'However' (contrast), 'Furthermore' (addition), 'Thus' (conclusion)
Wrong transitions confuse readers: Using 'Although' when 'Because' is needed changes meaning
Placement: Transition usually starts the new sentence to connect it to the prior idea
Common trap: Multiple transitions in one passage — only ONE fits logically

example.label: Transition Example
example.text: Previous sentence: 'Many love the new law.' Next: '[TRANS] some disagree.' RIGHT: However/Nevertheless. WRONG: Additionally (implies agreement)

slides.tip: Before picking a transition, reread the sentences around it to see the logical connection.

slides.title: 'NO CHANGE' Strategy
points: If the original text is grammatically correct AND clear, 'NO CHANGE' may be right
Don't fall for 'improve for the sake of improving' — clarity and correctness matter, not perfection
When all options seem similar, go with 'NO CHANGE' unless there's a clear error or better choice
Track 'NO CHANGE' answers across the section — if too many cluster, recheck
slides.tip: Many test-takers overlook 'NO CHANGE' — always consider it seriously.

slides.title: Common Grammar Traps & Mistakes
points: Its vs. It's: 'its' = possessive (Its color), 'it's' = contraction for 'it is'
Who vs. Whom: 'who' = subject, 'whom' = object (Whom did you see? = You saw whom?)
Affect vs. Effect: 'affect' = verb (to influence), 'effect' = noun (result)
Their vs. There vs. They're: Possessive, location, and contraction for 'they are'
slides.tip: These four pairs appear frequently — master them and you'll catch easy points.

slides.title: Rhetorical Questions: Relevance & Support
points: Relevance: Does the sentence support the main point? If not, delete it
Example insertion: 'Which choice best illustrates the author's claim?' — find the most specific example
Supporting details: Does the new sentence strengthen or weaken the paragraph's purpose?
Logical flow: Does it follow naturally from the prior sentence, or does it derail the argument?

example.label: Relevance Example
example.text: Paragraph about wildlife conservation: Option says 'Blue jays are common.' -> REMOVE (off-topic). Better: 'Some endangered species have doubled in population.'

slides.tip: Ask 'Does this sentence help prove the author's point?' If no, it doesn't belong.

slides.title: Adding & Revising Sentences
points: Adding a sentence: Check if it's relevant, doesn't repeat other sentences, and flows from the prior sentence
Revising a sentence: Compare the new version to the original — ask if it's clearer, shorter, or more appropriate
Delete option: Sometimes 'DELETE' is correct if the sentence is redundant, off-topic, or weakens the paragraph
Placement: A sentence might be correct but in the wrong spot — watch for that
slides.tip: Read the full paragraph before answering 'add/revise/delete' questions — context determines fit.

slides.title: Passage Structure & Purpose
points: Main idea: What is the author trying to prove or convey in the entire passage?
Paragraph purpose: Does each paragraph support, explain, or counter the main idea?
Concluding questions: Often ask about overall structure or the author's intent
Opening & closing: The first and last sentences hint at the passage's purpose
slides.tip: Skim each passage in 30 seconds to identify its main point before answering rhetorical questions.

slides.title: Style & Audience Awareness
points: Target audience shapes word choice: Scientific -> formal, memoir -> personal, blog -> casual
Author's purpose: Inform, persuade, entertain, explain — check word choice and tone for clues
Level of detail: Is the passage using technical jargon, simple language, or a mix?
Register shift: Switching from formal to casual (or vice versa) signals a problem
slides.tip: Before each passage, ask: 'Who is this written for and why?' Then match answers to that context.

slides.title: Scoring & Your English Score
points: English score (1–36) is independent; impacts your composite score equally with Math, Reading, Science
Each question worth ~0.48 points (75 questions = 36 points total)
Wrong answer = 0 points; skipped questions = 0 points (no penalty for guessing)
Aim: 70+ correct answers = 34+; 65+ = 32+; 60+ = 29+
slides.tip: Guess on every question you don't get to; wrong guesses don't lower your score.

slides.title: Test Day Mindset & Strategy
points: Anxiety management: Take deep breaths between passages; don't overthink any single question
Pacing check: At 22.5 min (halfway), you should be finishing passage 2.5
Guessing policy: Never leave a question blank — a guess has 20% chance vs. 0%
Mental stamina: English is first section; stay sharp and focused through all 5 passages
slides.tip: The first 10 minutes set your rhythm — nail those early passages to build confidence.

slides.title: Diagnostic: Find Your Weak Areas
points: Grammar errors: Count how many you miss per test — target these if >10 per test
Rhetorical skills: Do you lose more points on strategy or punctuation questions?
Passage type: Which passage style trips you up (narrative, formal essay, technical)?
Time management: Are you running out of time, or making careless mistakes in your rush?
slides.tip: Track misses by category (comma splices, modifiers, tone) to focus your review efficiently.

slides.title: Practice & Review Protocol
points: Timed practice: Always do full passages under time pressure — untimed practice doesn't build pacing
Review strategy: For each wrong answer, write down WHY it's wrong in one sentence
Error tracking: Keep a 'grammar errors' list — if you miss the same rule twice, drill it
Retake passages: Re-do hard passages 1 week later to check if you learned the pattern
slides.tip: Quality review > quantity of practice. One thoroughly reviewed test beats three skimmed tests.

slides.title: Next Steps & Free ACT Mock Test
points: Practice full passages under timed conditions (15 min/5 questions per passage)
Review every mistake — grammar or rhetorical? Make a list of recurring patterns
Take a free ACT mock test to track your progress and identify weak areas
Re-take weak sections after 1 week of targeted practice
slides.cta: Free ACT English Mock Test Available
slides.tip: Consistent practice beats cramming. Aim for 15 min/day, 5 days/week.

act-math.title: ACT Math — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
act-math.summary: Tackle 60 questions in 60 minutes using backsolving, plugging in, and strategic guessing.

slides.title: What is ACT Math?
points: 60 questions, 60 minutes (1 min/question average); calculator ALLOWED on all questions
Content: Pre-algebra, Elementary algebra, Intermediate algebra, Coordinate geometry, Plane geometry, Trigonometry
5 answer choices (A–E); questions ordered easy to hard (roughly)
Score range: 1–36 (equal weight on composite with English, Reading, Science)
slides.tip: The calculator is a tool, not a crutch — use it wisely, not for every arithmetic step.

slides.title: Time Management & Pacing
points: Questions 1–30: Easier; aim 20 seconds each (10 min total for 30 questions)
Questions 31–50: Medium; aim 1 min each (20 min total)
Questions 51–60: Hard; aim 1.5–2 min each or strategic guess (15 min left to attempt 10)
If stuck for 30 seconds, skip and return; don't waste time on one hard problem
slides.tip: Front-load the easier questions to build confidence and points. Rush through hard ones and come back if time.

slides.title: Backsolving (Testing Answers)
points: When unsure how to solve, plug each answer back into the problem — one will work
Start with (C) (middle choice) or (D) — eliminates half the range with one test
Saves time vs. solving algebraically if the algebra is messy
Works best for: Equations, word problems, and geometry where you can verify the answer

example.label: Backsolving Example
example.text: Find x: 2x + 5 = 17. Try (C) x=6: 2(6)+5=17? Yes! Answer: C.

slides.tip: Backsolving is fastest for late-section hard problems; less useful for early easy ones.

slides.title: Plugging In Numbers (Substitution)
points: If the problem has variables but answer choices are numbers, PLUG IN your own numbers for the variables
Pick simple, easy-to-work-with numbers: 2, 5, 10, or 100
Plug your numbers into each answer choice and see which matches your calculated result
Helpful for: Algebra, percentages, and word problems with unknown quantities

example.label: Plugging In Example
example.text: If x+y = 10 and x=2, which expresses y in terms of x? Try x=2: y=8. Test answers with x=2, see which gives y=8. Answer works!

slides.tip: Plugging in is faster and clearer than solving algebraically when dealing with complex expressions.

slides.title: Pre-Algebra & Number Properties
points: Factors, multiples, primes, integers, ratios, proportions, percentage
Order of operations (PEMDAS): Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract
Negative numbers: Negative × Negative = Positive; Negative + Positive = depends on magnitude
Decimals & fractions: Convert between them; be careful with place value

example.label: Percentage Example
example.text: What is 20% of 50? 20/100 × 50 = 10. Common mistake: Confusing percent increase vs. decrease.

slides.tip: If you're unsure, use your calculator — but make sure you set it up correctly.

slides.title: Elementary & Intermediate Algebra
points: Solving linear equations: Isolate the variable using inverse operations (add/subtract, multiply/divide)
Systems of equations: Solve for two unknowns using substitution or elimination
Quadratic equations: Factor or use the quadratic formula; know that x = (-b ± √(b²-4ac)) / 2a
Exponents & radicals: x^a × x^b = x^(a+b); √x × √y = √(xy); negative exponents = reciprocals

example.label: Quadratic Example
example.text: Solve: x² + 5x + 6 = 0. Factor: (x+2)(x+3)=0. Solutions: x = -2 or x = -3.

slides.tip: Factoring is faster than the quadratic formula on most ACT problems — practice it.

slides.title: Coordinate Geometry & Graphing
points: Slope: m = (y₂ - y₁) / (x₂ - x₁); positive = up-right, negative = down-right, zero = horizontal, undefined = vertical
Lines: y = mx + b (slope-intercept form); m = slope, b = y-intercept
Distance formula: d = √[(x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²]
Midpoint formula: Midpoint = [(x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2]

example.label: Slope Example
example.text: Line through (2,3) and (4,7): slope = (7-3)/(4-2) = 4/2 = 2. Equation: y = 2x + b; plug in (2,3): 3 = 2(2) + b, so b = -1. Line: y = 2x - 1.

slides.tip: Coordinate geometry questions often have diagrams — sketch the points on a graph if unsure.

slides.title: Plane Geometry: Angles & Triangles
points: Angles: Sum of angles in a triangle = 180°; sum in a quadrilateral = 360°
Parallel lines cut by a transversal: Corresponding angles are equal; alternate interior angles are equal
Triangle types: Right (90° angle), Isosceles (2 equal sides/angles), Equilateral (3 equal sides/angles, all 60°)
Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c² (right triangles only)

example.label: Triangle Angles Example
example.text: Triangle has angles 60° and 70°. Third angle = 180 - 60 - 70 = 50°.

slides.tip: Pythagorean theorem is heavily tested — know common triples (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17).

slides.title: Plane Geometry: Circles & Area
points: Circle: Radius (r), diameter (d = 2r), circumference (C = 2πr), area (A = πr²)
Area formulas: Triangle (½bh), Rectangle (l × w), Parallelogram (bh), Trapezoid (½(b₁+b₂)h), Circle (πr²)
Volume formulas: Cube (s³), Rectangular solid (l × w × h), Cylinder (πr²h), Sphere (⁴⁄₃πr³)
Surface area: Sum of all faces; cylinder = 2πr² + 2πrh

example.label: Area Example
example.text: Circle with radius 3: A = π(3)² = 9π ≈ 28.27 sq units. Circumference = 2π(3) = 6π.

slides.tip: Know the formulas; the test doesn't give them. Write them down at the start if you tend to forget.

slides.title: Trigonometry Basics
points: SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent
Special angles: 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles have known ratios (memorize!)
Inverse trig: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ to find angles when you know the ratio
Trig identities: sin² + cos² = 1; tan = sin/cos

example.label: Trig Example
example.text: Right triangle: opposite = 3, hypotenuse = 5. sin(θ) = 3/5. Find θ: θ = sin⁻¹(0.6) ≈ 37°.

slides.tip: Trig appears in ~5–10 questions. If it's not your strength, focus on easier algebra/geometry first.

slides.title: Word Problems: Setup & Strategy
points: Read twice: Once for overall meaning, once for specific numbers and what you're solving for
Translate words to math: 'is' = =, 'of' = ×, 'per' = ÷, 'more than' = +, 'less than' = -
Define variables clearly: Let x = the unknown quantity
Set up the equation, solve, and check: Plug your answer back into the problem

example.label: Word Problem Example
example.text: 'A store sells shirts for $15 each. If you buy 4 shirts, how much do you spend?' Setup: Cost = 15 × 4 = $60.

slides.tip: Word problems are just algebra in disguise. Break them into small pieces and translate each piece.

slides.title: Common Math Traps & Mistakes
points: Sign errors: Forgetting to distribute a negative or flip the inequality when multiplying by -1
Order of operations: Forgetting to do exponents before multiplication (2 + 3² = 11, not 25)
Misreading the question: The question asks for x, but you found 2x — double-check what's being asked
Approximation errors: Rounding mid-calculation and getting a slightly wrong answer
slides.tip: Before submitting an answer, ask: 'Does this make sense in context?' and 'Did I answer the right question?'

slides.title: Estimation & Eliminating Wrong Answers
points: Rough estimate: If the answer should be around 50 and the choices are 10, 50, 200, 500, 5000, eliminate extremes
Units: Watch for unit conversion (inches to feet, minutes to hours) — a common trap
Reasonableness: A negative answer to a 'how many items' problem is wrong; a probability > 1 is wrong
Eliminate first: Cross out clearly wrong answers before calculating exactly
slides.tip: Elimination narrows your guessing odds; even a smart guess beats a random one.

slides.title: Sequence & Series (Bonus Topic)
points: Arithmetic sequence: Same difference between terms (a, a+d, a+2d, ...); sum = n/2 × (first + last)
Geometric sequence: Same ratio between terms (a, ar, ar², ...); sum = a × (1 - rⁿ) / (1 - r)
Permutations & combinations: nPr (order matters) vs. nCr (order doesn't)
slides.tip: Sequences appear in ~1–3 questions; other topics are more heavily tested.

slides.title: Probability & Counting (Bonus Topic)
points: Probability: # favorable outcomes / # total outcomes; always between 0 and 1
Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B); 'and' means multiply
Dependent events: Order matters; adjust the denominator after each selection
Counting principle: If you have choices for A (n ways) and B (m ways), total = n × m
slides.tip: Probability is low-density on ACT Math (~1–2 questions); focus on algebra and geometry.

slides.title: Scoring & Your Math Score
points: Math score (1–36) is independent; equal weight in composite calculation
Each question worth ~0.6 points (60 questions = 36 points total)
No penalty for guessing; wrong answers = 0 points
Aim: 55+ correct = 32+; 50+ correct = 29+; 45+ correct = 26+
slides.tip: Skipping hard questions to save time is smart — guessing on late questions is better than leaving blanks.

slides.title: Test-Day Math Strategy
points: Read the question TWICE: Once to understand, once to identify what you're solving for
Calculator use: Use it for arithmetic, but NOT for setting up the problem — sketches and equations first
Check your setup: Before calculating, verify your equation/formula matches the question context
Pacing rule: If a question takes >2 min, skip it and come back; don't let one hard problem cost time
slides.tip: Accuracy on easy questions is more important than solving hard ones. Get the first 40 right before chasing the last 20.

slides.title: Common Careless Mistakes to Avoid
points: Misreading: The question asks for the area, but you calculated circumference — reread the final question
Sign errors: Negative signs in front of parentheses flip all signs inside (-(x+2) = -x-2)
Calculator errors: Forgetting parentheses: 5+3*2 = 11, not 16 (order of operations!)
Unit conversion: Answer is in dollars but question asks for cents — multiply by 100
slides.tip: Before finalizing an answer, scan the problem once more: Does my answer match what's being asked?

slides.title: Next Steps & Free ACT Mock Test
points: Practice timed sections: 15 min for ~15 questions (match the pacing of the real test)
Review every wrong answer: Algebra error, careless mistake, or concept gap?
Take a free full-length ACT mock test to diagnose weak content areas
Focus practice on your weaker topics: Trig, coordinate geometry, or quadratics?
slides.cta: Free ACT Math Mock Test Available
slides.tip: Consistent daily practice (30 min/day) beats cramming. Build speed and accuracy together.

act-reading.title: ACT Reading — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
act-reading.summary: Master 40 questions across 4 passages in 35 minutes using strategic skimming and line-reference skills.

slides.title: What is ACT Reading?
points: 40 questions, 35 minutes across 4 passages (~8.5 min per passage)
Passage types: Prose Fiction, Social Science, Humanities, Natural Science
Question types: Main idea, detail, inference, vocabulary-in-context, author's purpose/tone
Score range: 1–36 (equal weight in composite; reading fatigue can hurt performance)
slides.tip: Reading is endurance; pace yourself on the first two passages to save energy for passage 4.

slides.title: Time Management & Passage Strategy
points: Budget: ~2 min to skim passage, ~6 min to answer 10 questions = 8 min per passage
Skim strategy: Read intro, first paragraph, topic sentences, and last paragraph — skip dense middle sections
Question-first tactic: Read questions before passage? NO — you'll waste time hunting; skim first, then answer
Mark up: Underline main claim, circle key names/dates, bracket confusing passages for reference
slides.tip: If you're behind on pacing, move to the next passage. Guessing on 2 at the end beats slow accuracy on all.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension: Main Idea & Structure
points: Main idea: Why did the author write this? What's the central argument or theme?
Structure: Intro (thesis) -> Supporting evidence/examples -> Counter-argument or nuance -> Conclusion
Passage tone: Is the author argumentative, analytical, narrative, or humorous?
Purpose: Explain, persuade, inform, entertain, or critique?

example.label: Passage Structure Example
example.text: Fiction: Intro (setting, character) -> Conflict -> Rising action -> Climax -> Resolution. Nonfiction: Thesis -> Evidence -> Analysis -> Conclusion.

slides.tip: The first sentence of each paragraph often tells you its purpose; read those closely.

slides.title: Detail Questions & Line References
points: Detail questions: 'According to the passage, what did X do?' — answer is DIRECTLY in the passage
Line references: The question points to a specific line or paragraph — go there first and reread the context
Read around the reference: The answer is often 1–2 sentences before or after the cited line
Don't infer: On detail questions, match the passage exactly — eliminate answers that are close but wrong

example.label: Detail Question Example
example.text: Q: 'In line 15, what did the scientist discover?' A: Reread lines 10–20 and find the discovery mentioned. Pick the match.

slides.tip: Detail questions are the easiest — use them to build confidence and points. Use passage numbers as a GPS.

slides.title: Inference & Author's Intent Questions
points: Inference: What can be reasonably concluded from the passage? Go beyond what's stated but stay close
Support requirement: Every inference must have evidence in the passage; no outside knowledge
Author's purpose: Why did the author mention this detail? What does it support?
Tone: Is the author approving, critical, neutral, sarcastic? Word choice reveals intent

example.label: Inference Example
example.text: Passage: 'The key hung on the wall untouched for years.' Inference: The key wasn't used often (reasonable) vs. The key opens a locked room (no evidence). First is better.

slides.tip: On inference questions, pick the answer that's most directly supported by the passage, not the most clever one.

slides.title: Vocabulary-in-Context Questions
points: Word definition: Test your understanding of the word AS USED IN THE PASSAGE, not the dictionary definition
Context clue: Look at surrounding sentences — they hint at meaning (cause/effect, contrast, restatement)
Multiple meanings: Many words have 2+ meanings (e.g., 'bank' = financial institution or river edge) — pick the contextual one
Eliminate: Denotation (literal meaning) is sometimes right, but connotation (feeling/implication) often matters

example.label: Vocab-in-Context Example
example.text: Sentence: 'The project ran into resistance from the committee.' Does 'resistance' mean (A) opposition (B) force opposing motion (C) electrical property? Answer: (A) opposition (fits the human context).

slides.tip: Always reread the sentence with each answer choice plugged in; hear how it sounds.

slides.title: Contrast & Comparison in Passage Analysis
points: Contrasts: 'However,' 'yet,' 'but,' 'although' signal a shift — note what's being opposed
Comparisons: 'Similarly,' 'like,' 'both' signal parallel ideas — identify the shared quality
Author's bias: Does the author favor one side or show both perspectives? This hints at purpose
Nuance: Sometimes the author agrees with a criticism but then clarifies — catch the 'but' that shifts meaning

example.label: Contrast Example
example.text: Passage: 'Early critics dismissed the theory. However, recent evidence supports it.' Author's intent: Early dismissal was wrong; now vindicated. This nuance matters on questions.

slides.tip: When you see a contrast word, pause and reread carefully — the author is telling you something important.

slides.title: Prose Fiction Strategy (Narrative)
points: Character motive: Why does the character act? Look for clues in dialogue and internal thought
Conflict: External (character vs. other/environment) vs. internal (character vs. self/emotions)
Setting & mood: Time, place, and atmosphere shape the story's meaning
Point of view: First person (I/we), third person (he/she) — affects what the reader knows

example.label: Fiction Example
example.text: Character avoids eye contact and mumbles answers. Why? Inference: shy, anxious, or hiding something. Reread dialogue for clues.

slides.tip: Fiction passages test inference and tone heavily. Focus on what the character does and says, not just events.

slides.title: Social Science Strategy (History, Psychology, Sociology)
points: Thesis-first: The author makes a claim and supports it with evidence and examples
Evidence types: Historical facts, statistics, expert quotes, research findings, case studies
Argument structure: Does the author use cause-effect, comparison, or problem-solution?
Time: Pay attention to dates and historical context — things change over time

example.label: Social Science Example
example.text: Passage argues that immigration drives economic growth. Evidence: historical data, economist quotes, statistics. Questions test whether you traced the argument.

slides.tip: Social science passages are dense — underline the thesis and 2–3 main supporting points. That's all you need.

slides.title: Humanities Strategy (Literature, Art, Philosophy)
points: Author's interpretation: What does the author argue about the book, art, or philosophy?
Evidence: Quotations, themes, symbolism, and historical context support the interpretation
Judgment: Does the author admire, critique, or analytically examine the work?
Nuance: Humanities passages often have 'on the other hand' — the author acknowledges complexity

example.label: Humanities Example
example.text: Passage analyzes a poem's use of color. Author argues color = emotional turmoil. Questions ask what color represents and why the author interprets it that way.

slides.tip: Humanities passages are interpretive. The 'right' answer is the one the author defends, not your opinion.

slides.title: Natural Science Strategy (Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Earth Science)
points: Process or mechanism: How does something work? Identify steps and relationships
Definition clarity: Scientific terms are precise — distinguish subtle differences (heat vs. temperature)
Evidence: Data, experiments, observations support the theory
Scope: Does the principle apply everywhere or under specific conditions?

example.label: Natural Science Example
example.text: Passage explains photosynthesis: Light -> energy -> glucose. Questions test understanding of the process, not memorized facts.

slides.tip: Natural science passages are logical. If you trace the cause-effect flow, you'll answer most questions without rereading.

slides.title: Eliminating Wrong Answers on Reading Questions
points: Out of scope: Answer mentions something not in the passage — eliminate
Opposite: Answer contradicts what the passage says — eliminate
Too extreme: 'Always,' 'never,' 'all,' 'none' are risky; look for qualified language
Right idea, wrong reason: The answer is true but the justification is wrong — eliminate

example.label: Wrong Answer Example
example.text: Passage: 'The study suggests that exercise may improve mood.' Wrong: 'The study proves exercise always improves mood.' (Too extreme; 'may' != 'always')

slides.tip: If you're stuck, eliminate the obviously wrong answers first; your odds of guessing right improve.

slides.title: Pacing Trouble & Recovery
points: If you're behind: Skip the hardest questions (often inference/tone) and do detail questions first
Last passage panic: If you have <2 min left, skim the questions, make strategic guesses, and move on
Build speed: Practice passages under timed conditions; aim to finish in 7–8 min, not 10–12
Flag hard questions: Mark them as you go so you can return after finishing all passages
slides.tip: Speed comes from familiarity, not rushing. Do practice passages 3–4 times per week to train your brain.

slides.title: Scoring & Your Reading Score
points: Reading score (1–36) is independent; equal weight in composite with English, Math, Science
Each question worth ~0.9 points (40 questions = 36 points total)
No penalty for guessing; wrong answers = 0 points
Aim: 36+ correct = 34+; 32+ correct = 31+; 28+ correct = 27+
slides.tip: Reading is hardest to improve quickly; consistent practice over weeks builds comprehension speed.

slides.title: Passage Type Quick Reference
points: Prose Fiction: Focus on character motivation, conflict, tone changes — less detail, more inference
Social Science: Main argument + evidence structure — identify thesis and supporting examples
Humanities: Author's interpretation + evaluation — understand critical viewpoint, not just facts
Natural Science: Process/mechanism + data support — causation, not just information
slides.tip: Knowing what each passage type emphasizes helps you skip irrelevant details and zoom in on key ideas.

slides.title: Building Reading Stamina
points: Read actively: Underline, annotate, restate ideas in your head — passive reading causes mind-drift
First passage setup: Don't rush passage 1 to 'bank' time — set a steady pace and stick to it
Mental fatigue: By passage 4, your brain is tired — expect inference questions to feel harder
Recovery technique: If you zone out mid-passage, take 10 seconds to refocus before continuing
slides.tip: Reading stamina improves with practice. The more passages you do under timed conditions, the stronger you get.

slides.title: Diagnostic: Your Reading Weak Spot
points: Detail vs. Inference: Do you miss easy line-reference questions or harder inference questions?
Passage type: Do you struggle with fiction (emotion/motivation) or technical prose (dense info)?
Time management: Running out of time on passage 4, or rushing and making careless mistakes?
Vocabulary: Stuck on vocab-in-context? Review word meanings and context clue types
slides.tip: Track which question types you miss most — focus your practice on that category, not all passages equally.

slides.title: Next Steps & Free ACT Mock Test
points: Practice one passage at a time: Skim, answer questions, review misses, then move to next
Time yourself: Aim for 8–9 min per passage; track which passage type (fiction vs. science) is slowest
Identify patterns: Do you struggle with inference, vocab, or detail? Focus practice accordingly
Take a free full-length ACT mock test to simulate real test conditions and pacing

act-science.title: ACT Science — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
act-science.summary: Conquer 40 questions in 35 minutes by reading data first, finding trends, and comparing experimental designs.

slides.title: What is ACT Science?
points: 40 questions, 35 minutes across 6–7 passages (~5 min per passage); NO outside science knowledge needed
Passage types: Data Representation (graphs/tables), Research Summaries (experiments), Conflicting Viewpoints (competing theories)
Test reasoning from data, NOT memorized facts — interpret tables, graphs, and experimental results
Score range: 1–36 (equal weight in composite; poorest predictor of college science performance)
slides.tip: ACT Science is a reading & reasoning test, not a science test. You don't need chemistry or biology knowledge.

slides.title: Time Management & Passage Strategy
points: Budget: ~5 min per passage (1 min to read, 4 min to answer ~5–6 questions)
Read the DATA FIRST, then the passage: Graphs and tables are the question source, not prose
Skim passage prose: It provides context and explains the experiment; don't memorize details
Mark key features: Axis labels, units, legends, and data patterns; these answer most questions
slides.tip: Science test-takers often waste time reading prose. Skip directly to the graphs and tables; they tell the story.

slides.title: Data Representation Passages: Reading Graphs & Tables
points: Axes: X-axis (independent variable, what changes) vs. Y-axis (dependent variable, what's measured)
Units & scale: Voltage, temperature, moles, seconds — units matter for comparisons
Trends: Is the line rising, falling, flat, or curved? When does it change direction?
Multiple lines/variables: Compare trends across conditions; note where lines intersect or diverge

example.label: Graph Reading Example
example.text: Graph: X = Temperature (°C), Y = Enzyme activity (%). Trend: Activity rises 20–40°C, peaks at 40°C, drops 40–80°C. Q: 'At what temp is activity highest?' Answer: 40°C (read peak on Y-axis).

slides.tip: Tables are just data in rows/columns — same reading skill as graphs. Find the row/column intersection.

slides.title: Data Representation: Interpolation & Extrapolation
points: Interpolation: Estimating a value BETWEEN two data points (the graph line between two plotted points)
Extrapolation: Predicting a value BEYOND the shown data (extending the trend off the graph)
Caution: Extrapolation assumes the trend continues; real data often changes outside the measured range
Straight line vs. curve: Assume trends continue as shown; don't invent bends or breaks

example.label: Interpolation Example
example.text: Graph shows points at X=10, Y=20 and X=20, Y=40. Q: 'Estimate Y when X=15.' Answer: Midpoint = Y=30 (linear interpolation).

slides.tip: If a graph shows a clear trend, extend it mentally to answer prediction questions.

slides.title: Research Summary Passages: Experimental Design
points: Research question: What is the experiment testing? (Usually stated at the start)
Variables: Independent (what the experimenter changes), dependent (what's measured), control (unchanged baseline)
Setup: How many trials? What conditions? What's held constant?
Results: Did the hypothesis hold? What do the data show?

example.label: Experiment Example
example.text: Study: Does pH affect enzyme activity? Change pH (independent) -> measure enzyme activity (dependent) -> control is neutral pH. Results show peak activity at pH 7. Q: 'What is the control?' Answer: Neutral pH condition.

slides.tip: Identify the independent variable FIRST — it's usually the answer to 'what did they change?'

slides.title: Research Summaries: Comparing Experiments
points: Multiple experiments: Different setups testing the same question; compare what changed between them
Experiment differences: A changed condition (heat, pH, concentration); B added a new variable; C expanded the range
Consistency: Do multiple experiments reach the same conclusion? Strengthens the claim
Limitations: Did one experiment fail to test something? Questions often ask this

example.label: Comparing Experiments Example
example.text: Exp 1: pH 5–9. Exp 2: pH 5–12. Q: 'How does Exp 2 improve on Exp 1?' Answer: Exp 2 tests a wider pH range (extends knowledge).

slides.tip: When comparing experiments, ask: 'What did Exp 2 do differently/better?' That's often the answer.

slides.title: Conflicting Viewpoints: Comparing Theories
points: Two or three competing explanations for the same phenomenon — one may be correct, both partially right, or context-dependent
Viewpoint summaries: Read each theory's key claims and supporting reasoning
Points of agreement: Both theories might agree on some facts but disagree on interpretation
Points of disagreement: Identify WHERE and WHY the theories diverge
Evidence: Which theory's claims are supported by the data presented?

example.label: Viewpoint Example
example.text: Theory A: Dinosaurs went extinct due to meteor impact. Theory B: Volcanic eruptions caused extinction. Both agree extinction occurred; differ on cause. Q: 'Which theory is best supported by fossil evidence?' Answer: Look at the provided evidence; determine which it favors.

slides.tip: Conflicting Viewpoints passages test your ability to evaluate competing claims — stay neutral and let the data decide.

slides.title: Conflicting Viewpoints: Finding Support & Weaknesses
points: Supporting evidence: Which facts or observations back each theory? (Data may favor one over the other)
Weaknesses: What assumption does each theory make? What evidence could refute it?
Plausibility: Is each theory consistent with known science? (Don't use outside knowledge; evaluate based on passage info)
New data: If new information is presented, which theory does it support or contradict?

example.label: Support Example
example.text: New evidence: High iridium levels in rocks (meteorite marker). Q: 'Which theory is now more likely?' Answer: Theory A (meteor impact) — iridium supports it.

slides.tip: On 'new data' questions, reread the theory statements and ask: 'Would this evidence support or contradict it?'

slides.title: Data & Variables: Identifying Relationships
points: Positive correlation: As one variable increases, the other increases (upward trend)
Negative correlation: As one increases, the other decreases (downward trend)
No correlation: No relationship; data scattered randomly
Causal vs. correlational: Correlation != causation (both might depend on a third factor)

example.label: Correlation Example
example.text: Graph: Temperature (X) vs. Ice cream sales (Y). Positive correlation: hotter days lead to more sales. But causation? Heat causes sales, not vice versa.

slides.tip: ACT doesn't ask about causation explicitly, but correlation questions assume: correlation direction = variable relationship.

slides.title: Common ACT Science Question Types
points: Reading graphs: 'According to the graph, as X increases, Y...' — trace the line/trend
Interpolation/extrapolation: 'Estimate Y when X = ...' — find or predict the value
Hypothesis & data fit: 'Which result best supports the hypothesis?' — match data to prediction
Experiment design: 'What is the control/variable/limitation?' — identify experimental structure
Comparing viewpoints: 'Which theory explains the data best?' — evaluate support for each
slides.tip: Most questions ask: 'What does the data show?' Focus on the numbers, not your science knowledge.

slides.title: Avoiding Traps & Misreadings
points: Axis confusion: Did you read X vs. Y correctly? Swapping axes reverses your answer
Unit mismatch: Is the answer in °C or K? cm or m? Always check units in the graph/question
Scale misreading: Linear vs. logarithmic scale changes how you interpret data (log scale compresses large ranges)
Outside knowledge: Don't inject what you 'know' from chemistry class — answer ONLY from the passage

example.label: Trap Example
example.text: Q: 'When temperature = 50, what is pH?' You skim and see pH=7. But the axis label says 'Temperature (°C) vs. Pressure (atm).' You read the WRONG axis!

slides.tip: Before answering, say aloud: 'X-axis = ?, Y-axis = ?' This catches axis swaps.

slides.title: Pacing & Guessing Strategy
points: If behind: Skip Conflicting Viewpoints (hardest, ~6 questions) and focus on Data Rep (easiest, ~15 questions)
Time left <1 min: Make educated guesses on remaining questions based on trends you see in data
Easy questions first: Answer fact-based 'read the graph' questions before inference-heavy ones
Flag and return: Mark ambiguous questions and revisit after completing all other passages
slides.tip: Science passages are more forgiving for time — you don't need to fully 'understand' experiments, just read data.

slides.title: Scoring & Your Science Score
points: Science score (1–36) is independent; equal weight in composite with English, Math, Reading
Each question worth ~0.9 points (40 questions = 36 points total)
No penalty for guessing; wrong answers = 0 points
Aim: 36+ correct = 34+; 32+ correct = 31+; 28+ correct = 27+
slides.tip: Science is learnable quickly — focus on graph-reading and experimental design, not memorizing science.

slides.title: Data Pitfalls: False Patterns & Trends
points: Assume continuity: Just because data shows one trend doesn't mean it continues forever — be cautious on extrapolation
Curve vs. line: Is the trend truly linear, or is it curved? Misreading the curve shape leads to wrong extrapolations
Sample bias: Limited data (e.g., only 2 data points) might not represent the full pattern — watch the sample size
Noise: Small fluctuations don't mean the trend changed; look for large, consistent changes
slides.tip: When a question asks 'predict when X=100,' check: Is the trend linear? Does it extend that far in the shown data?

slides.title: Experimental Design Red Flags
points: Confounding variables: If the experiment doesn't control for an alternative cause, the result is ambiguous
Sample size: A study with only 5 subjects is weaker than one with 500 — sample size affects confidence
Replication: Can other labs repeat the experiment? ACT sometimes asks if results are reproducible
Bias: Are the experimenters favoring one result over another? Blind studies avoid this

example.label: Confounding Example
example.text: Study: Does coffee improve mood? But subjects also exercised (which improves mood). Confounding variable: exercise. Can't isolate coffee's effect.

slides.tip: On 'experimental design' questions, ask: 'What variable might they have missed that could explain the result?'

slides.title: Interpreting Conflicting Viewpoints Carefully
points: Don't pick your favorite: Choose the theory BEST SUPPORTED BY THE DATA, not the one you like
Partial truth: Both theories might be partly correct — look for which is MORE supported by evidence
Scope matters: Theory A might be correct at low temperatures, Theory B at high temperatures — context is key
Missing evidence: A theory isn't wrong just because it's not tested — look for direct contradiction, not absence of proof
slides.tip: If two theories both seem plausible, re-examine the passage data — it will favor one over the other.

slides.title: Diagnostic: Your Science Weak Spot
points: Data reading: Struggle with graphs? Tables? Practice axis labels, scales, and trend identification
Experimental design: Confused by control groups, variables, or confounds? Drill these concepts
Conflicting Viewpoints: Hard to pick between theories? Review how evidence supports/contradicts each
Time pressure: Can't finish in 5 min per passage? Practice skimming prose and jumping straight to graphs
slides.tip: Science is the fastest to improve — focus on your weakest passage type (Data Rep, Research, or Viewpoints).

slides.title: Next Steps & Free ACT Mock Test
points: Practice one passage at a time: Read data first, answer questions, review misses for data-reading errors
Identify weak spots: Do graphs confuse you? Experimental design? Conflicting Viewpoints? Practice those
Take a free full-length ACT mock test under timed conditions to simulate real test pacing
Build speed: Aim for 5 min per passage; the faster you read data, the more time for hard questions
